history.note: For development and automated tests only. Not real course content.

title: [Dev] Capstone test
intro: In this self-directed project, you pick one UN Sustainable Development Goal (SDG), define a problem through an economist's eyes, and propose a realistic solution.
This isn't a graded assignment. It's a project you complete on your own. Use the rubric to check your work, and ask the AI coach questions if you want.
Submitting it does not count as an official academic grade or certification.

steps.title: 1. Choose an SDG
steps.guidance: Pick one SDG that interests you and write why you chose it.

fields.label: Why you chose this SDG
fields.help: Connect it to your own experience or interests.

steps.title: 2. Define the economic problem
steps.guidance: Be specific: whose problem is it, and what scarcity or choice is involved? Narrowing it to one place or one market helps.

fields.label: Problem definition
fields.help: What is the problem, and why is it an economic problem?

steps.title: 3. Economic concepts and evidence
steps.guidance: Write down the economic concepts that explain the problem (supply and demand, externalities, opportunity cost, etc.) and the evidence you checked yourself. When you use numbers, include the source (title, publisher, date).

fields.label: Related economic concepts
fields.help: Name each concept and explain how it works in this problem.

fields.label: Evidence and sources
fields.help: Title, publisher, and date of each source you checked yourself. Leave out any numbers you could not verify.

steps.title: 4. Stakeholders
steps.guidance: List the people and groups affected by this problem and where each one stands.

fields.label: Stakeholders and their positions
fields.help: Consumers, producers, government, future generations, etc.

steps.title: 5. Incentives and trade-offs
steps.guidance: Describe the incentives (gains and costs) each stakeholder responds to and the trade-offs involved.

fields.label: Incentives and trade-offs
fields.help: Choices between efficiency and equity, now and the future, costs and benefits

steps.title: 6. Propose a solution
steps.guidance: Propose a realistic solution (a policy, an institution, or a change in behavior) and compare it with other options.

fields.label: Solution and comparison with alternatives
fields.help: Your proposed approach and the alternatives you compared it with

steps.title: 7. Evaluate costs, benefits, and limits
steps.guidance: Write down the expected costs and benefits of your solution, who pays, and its limits and uncertainties.

fields.label: Costs, benefits, and limits
fields.help: Who gains and who pays? What assumptions does it rely on?

steps.title: 8. Final proposal
steps.guidance: Using your earlier steps, write a proposal that a reader can easily follow.

fields.label: Final proposal
fields.help: In this order: problem → evidence → solution → costs and benefits → limits

steps.title: 9. Reflect
steps.guidance: Write what you learned, what changed your mind, and what you want to explore further.

fields.label: Reflection
fields.help: What did you learn, and what would you do differently next time?

rubric.note: These are suggested criteria and weights. They are provisional until a human (platform admin) reviews them, and they are a self-check tool, not an official score.

criteria.name: Accuracy of economic concepts
criteria.description: Are economic concepts used correctly and applied to the problem?

descriptors.1: Concepts are missing or used incorrectly.
descriptors.2: Partly there, but some parts are missing or inaccurate.
descriptors.4: Uses concepts correctly and explains how the problem works.

criteria.name: Problem definition
criteria.description: Is the scope clear, and is it framed as an economic problem?

descriptors.2: Partly there, but some parts are missing or inaccurate.
descriptors.4: The scope, the people affected, and the causes are clear.

criteria.name: Quality of evidence
criteria.description: Does it give checked evidence and sources, and flag claims that could not be verified?

descriptors.1: There is no evidence or source.
descriptors.2: Partly there, but some parts are missing or inaccurate.
descriptors.4: Uses clearly sourced evidence and states its limits.

criteria.name: Stakeholder analysis
criteria.description: Does it cover the affected groups and their positions?

descriptors.2: Partly there, but some parts are missing or inaccurate.
descriptors.4: Gives balanced attention to the positions and interests of several groups.

criteria.name: Incentives and trade-offs
criteria.description: Are incentives and trade-offs explained in economic terms?

descriptors.2: Partly there, but some parts are missing or inaccurate.
descriptors.4: Clearly explains the key trade-offs and incentives.

criteria.name: Feasibility of the solution
criteria.description: Does it propose a realistic solution after weighing costs, benefits, and limits?

descriptors.1: The solution is unrealistic or not evaluated.
descriptors.2: Partly there, but some parts are missing or inaccurate.
descriptors.4: Weighs costs, benefits, and limits against alternatives.

criteria.name: Connection to the SDG
criteria.description: Are the problem and solution clearly linked to the chosen SDG?

descriptors.1: The link to the SDG is weak.
descriptors.2: Partly there, but some parts are missing or inaccurate.
descriptors.4: Explains the link at the level of specific SDG targets.

criteria.name: Communication and reflection
criteria.description: Is the proposal easy to read, and does it reflect on what was learned?

descriptors.2: Partly there, but some parts are missing or inaccurate.
